The partition key determines how items are distributed across physical partitions; items with the same partition key value form a logical partition so related data stays co‑located, making queries within that partition efficient and scoping transactions to a single logical partition [1]. A good partition key also helps spread storage and request volume evenly (high cardinality) to avoid hot partitions [2].

Use Azure Service Bus for the messaging layer and run the worker in Azure Container Apps with a KEDA scale rule.

- Azure Service Bus: a fully managed message broker with queues for competing consumers and classic work-distribution scenarios (order processing, pipelines) and supports retries/ dead-lettering to handle poison messages [3][1][5].  
- Azure Container Apps + KEDA: Container Apps supports KEDA-based autoscaling and can use a Service Bus queue-depth scale rule so the worker scales out as the queue deepens and back to zero when the queue drains; Container Apps can scale to zero and incur no compute charges while at zero replicas [2][8].

This combination is the canonical pattern to scale with queue depth and cost nothing when idle [2][8].

Availability zones are the recommended way to achieve redundancy: the reliability pillar advises deploying redundant instances across fault domains, and within a region availability zones are physically separate data centers so a zone‑redundant deployment keeps a workload available when a single zone fails [2]. For example, Container Apps can be deployed zone‑redundant so replicas are spread across zones and the loss of one zone does not take the application down [1]. This aligns with the reliability principle to design for failure and make faults survivable rather than trying to prevent them entirely [3].
